chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
title: Walter Brown and the first Decca session in Dallas
summary: He found singer Walter Brown on 18th Street and in ten days rehearsed Hootie Blues and Confessing the Blues for the Decca session, where Dave Kapp wanted blues and boogie.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: All right, now, let's hear a little bit about the band in Kansas City before you left to go to New York and we haven't discussed Walter Brown either.

Yes. Well, truthfully, before we went to New York, the big band, we -- when we made our first recordings, we went to Dallas, Texas. Walter Brown -- now, how I got Walter Brown, I happened to be high one night and I came through 18th Street and Walter Brown was singing the blues, and I listened to him sing the blues and I didn't have but 50 cents in my pocket and we were already scheduled to record for Decca. But I went back up to him and told him, I says, "Look, man, sing that song again." He sang that number again and I sit and listened to it.
So I went back to him, I says, "Look, I'll tell you what. You know I gave you my last 50 cents. Give me 25 cents back because I got to get me a bowl of chili." so he did.

He laughed. He said, "Man, I knew it was your last 50 cents. Here, here's a quarter." So here's what we did. I says, "Man, you want to record?" He says, "Yeah." I said, "I tell you what. We'll get together and get some blues together. We only got a matter of a few days to do it. But we'll get together and get these blues together and get them ready because we're going to record. We're going to Dallas." I think we only had ten to 12 days before we went to Dallas. I told him, "We only got about ten or 12 days and then we're going to Dallas and we're going to record."
So he says, "Yeah, I'm for it." I says, "Look we start rehearsing tomorrow." So what we did, we already had

"Hootie" blues, you know, that the band was playing. So I says, "Let's get together and get some words together for "Hootie" blues." So it wasn't but three choruses on the "Hootie" Blues, you know, that he had to do, and the rest was Bird blowing into the -- whatever was happening, you know.

Well, we got the words to that together and then we got "Confessing the Blues" together and I think the other one was -- well, we had a couple more blues. But those were the two that we recorded on the first thing and so when we went down there to do the record session, we had all kind of tunes like "Yardbird Suite" and stuff like that that we was going to cut with the band and which was that kind of -- I wished that I had the money. I would have had all that stuff cut, you know.

But anyway, nevertheless, the way fate put it, we played about two hours trying to get something that Dave Capp would take. He kept telling us, "Fellas, I can't make no money with that." So he finally says,-- I had forgotten I had Walter Brown there, see?
So all those good band numbers he knew, he didn't think he could market them, huh?
No, he said, "We can't market them because first of all, it's good, but I can't sell it." So he says -- and "can you play some boogie-woogie?" I says,

"Yeah." He says, "Play boogie-woogie." So we did, "Vine Street Boogie." He says, "Can you play some blues?" I says, "Yeah." The "Vine Street Boogie?" Vine Street must have been in the other session. But I think we did "Hootie Blues" first.

Then we followed up with "Confessing the Blues." And then he says -- yeah, we did do "Vine Street." "Vine Street Boogie." And then he says, "I'll take one of them other tunes," which was "Swingmatism." He says, after we did the two blues, he says, "Do a boogie and I'll take one of them other tunes," and he took "Swingmatism."
So we was mad, you know, because we didn't get to cut what we wanted to cut. But nevertheless, boom. Well, the real seller turned out to be the "Confessing the Blues" and the "Hootie Blues."
Was "Confessing the Blues" at the first session?
That was in the first one.
